idiom_name: Map/WeakMap store with an explicit bounded policy (no cache class)
implementation_notes: The classic cache object collapses into a built-in key store: Map preserves insertion order, so a manual max-size policy evicts the oldest key via store.keys().next().value, and has()/get() distinguish a missing entry from a stored undefined. When keys are objects whose lifetime should follow the object itself (per-DOM-node state, bound callbacks, per-request context), WeakMap gives GC-owned lifetime for free - at the cost of no size, no iteration and no TTL. TTL comes from a lazy expiry check on read (or a per-entry timer, which is heavier), and performance.now() avoids wall-clock jumps. The pattern's polymorphism - pluggable eviction, stores, statistics - lives in the wrapper you write, not in the language.
pitfalls: A Map holds strong references: without an eviction bound the cache is a memory leak - in a Node process it is unbounded, and in a long-lived SPA tab it pins DOM-adjacent objects.
One timer per entry keeps the event loop (or the browser's timer queue) busy and pins closures; lazy expiry on read is usually the better trade.
TTL is not invalidation: a write through another path leaves the entry valid until expiry, so every writer must delete the key.
Object keys are compared by identity: cached({id: 1}, ...) called twice never reuses an entry - key by a canonical string instead.
